title: 2025-06-12-quantized-embeddings-throughput-slo-alignment-prod-review
summary: Deep technical conversation on embedding dimensionality, quantization, batching, and rerank architecture to meet 100ms P95 latency SLO for a 2-stage search+rerank flow. Covered tradeoffs (1536 vs 768 dims), int8 quantization vs float32, batch sizing for GPU vs CPU, KV cache for prefixing repeated queries, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed on pilot benchmark approach and follow-ups.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-12 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~62 minutes | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Alex (BlueRiver Data Lead), Priya (ML Eng), Markus (Infra)

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick agenda: embeddings dims, quantization, batching, and then we want to align on the pilot benchmarks to prove out your 100ms P95 SLO for user rerank.

[00:28] Alex (BlueRiver): Yeah thanks, Sofia. Our goal: sub-100ms P95 on product search rerank for top-10 results. Current system is Elastic + a small re-ranker on CPU that takes ~300-400ms P95, so we need ~3x improvement.

[00:56] Daniel (Redwood SE): Got it. Quick question about your current vector store — approx cardinality and dims?

[01:05] Priya (ML Eng): We have 6.2M vectors, 1536 dims, stored as float32. We recently toyed with 768 but saw some drop in recall on tail queries.

[01:26] Markus (Infra): Also important: everything must run inside our VPC, keys in our KMS; on-prem eventual possibility.

[01:40] Daniel (SE): Makes sense. Two immediate levers: reduce vector dimensionality (1536->768), and quantize (float32 -> int8 or QAT). Both trade precision for memory and throughput. For index memory: 1536*4 bytes ~6KB per vector -> ~36GB for 6M vectors in dense form (rough calc — depends on index overhead). Int8 reduces by ~4x.

[02:12] Alex: That matches our back-of-envelope. But recall is the risk — we care about top-10 quality.

[02:28] Daniel: Right. For rerank architecture we usually recommend a two-stage flow: cheap ANN search (quantized index, 512-768 projection) to get top-K, then re-rank with full-dim scores or a cross-encoder. That keeps per-query cost low while protecting quality.

[02:48] Priya: Two-stage sounds good. What's the latency budget split? If 100ms total, maybe 30ms search + 60ms rerank + overhead?

[03:00] Sofia: Exactly — Daniel, can you walk through realistic latencies we see on Redwood Dedicated GPUs for both stages with batch sizing?

[03:12] Daniel: Sure. From our benchmarks: an int8 ANN lookup for a single query in a tuned FAISS-like index on a V100/RTX-class GPU can be sub-5ms for K=100 with optimized kernel and warm caches. Transfer+RPC overhead ~5-10ms depending on routing. For the re-rank: a dense dot-product re-ranker on a single GPU for 10 vectors at 1536 dims is often ~8-12ms if batched. Cross-encoder models are heavier — 50-120ms depending on model size.

[03:46] Markus: So for safety we should plan for 40ms ANN + 40ms rerank + 20ms buffer? That's already pushing 100ms.

[03:56] Daniel: You can improve by batching across nearby user requests — continuous batching up to a point. Our runtime has adaptive batching: if you accept slightly higher variance we can amortize expensive ops across N requests. But for low P95 SLOs you need strict limits.

[04:21] Alex: What batch sizes do you recommend? Our traffic is spiky but peak QPS is around 120 qps for the US region.

[04:33] Daniel: For GPU re-rankers at 1536 dims, sweet spot tends to be batch 16-64 depending on sequence lengths and model. For simple dot-product re-rank, batch 32 gives good throughput with minimal latency increase when GPU is local. At 120 qps, if you batch 32 you need enough concurrency to assemble batches without adding wait time — so routing and worker concurrency matter.

[04:58] Priya: If we can't reliably assemble batches, is CPU fallback viable?

[05:06] Daniel: CPU dot-products for 1536 dims scale poorly; latency will be higher — often 3-5x slower per item vs GPU. For strict 100ms P95, CPU-only is risky unless vectors are smaller (512 dims) or quantized heavily.

[05:28] Alex: How does KV cache help here? We have many repeated queries and personalized prefixes.

[05:35] Daniel: KV cache helps more for generation workloads, but for prefix caching of vectorized queries you can cache recent embeddings or top-K search results per user. Redwood supports prefix/KV caching; if a query repeats within the cache TTL you bypass compute entirely. In our tests, caching can reduce compute by 25-40% for high reuse workloads.

[05:58] Markus: For security we need cache encrypted in our VPC. Redwood Private supports customer-side KMS — we can configure SSE with our KMS keys.

[06:08] Sofia: We'll note that. Back to quantization: Daniel, what quality loss do you typically see moving from 1536 float32 to int8?

[06:18] Daniel: Varies by dataset. On semantic search benchmarks, int8 or product-quantization (PQ) can introduce a 0.5-4% drop in recall@10. Dimensionality reduction to 768 often costs a bit more — ~2-6% depending on the task. A common pattern: use a quantized index for the ANN stage and keep high-precision vectors for the small re-rank set.

[06:46] Priya: So keep the full precision vectors on cold storage and only load for re-rank? Storage cost then higher but compute minimal.

[06:54] Daniel: Exactly. Many customers store float32 for the golden set and keep a PQ or int8 index for lookup. That hybrid approach minimizes memory on the live index while preserving re-rank quality.

[07:08] Alex: Can Redwood route top-K search to a different model variant if GPU capacity is constrained? E.g., fall back to a smaller 768 model?

[07:18] Daniel: Yes, our smart routing supports version and variant fallback. You can set policies: prefer low latency, or prefer low cost, with automated fallback to smaller variants or different regions.

[07:30] Sofia: Let's talk cost numbers — rough order of magnitude for us. Alex, you have 120 qps peak, 6M vectors, top-K=50, re-rank top-10. Daniel, give a per-million-query infra cost estimate for GPU-backed two-stage flow vs hosted dedicated CPU fallback.

[07:46] Daniel: Quick roughs: GPU-backed two-stage (ANN on int8 GPU + GPU re-rank) amortized, you might see infra cost in the low tens of dollars per 100k queries if you run dedicated capacity with good batching. For CPU-only re-rank at tail loads, cost can be several x higher and latency worse. These numbers depend heavily on batch hit-rate and cache reuse. We'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet with detailed line items.

[08:20] Priya: Please attach the spreadsheet. We need per-1M query and per-month projections.

[08:27] Daniel: We'll share: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1-example-benchmark-embeddings (demo link) — contains perf runs on RTX A5000 and c6i-style CPU baselines, quantized vs float32, batch curves.

[08:40] Alex: Great. Another question: for on-prem how different is setup? Do we still get the same optimized kernels?

[08:48] Daniel: On-prem you can run Redwood Private where the control plane is customer-managed; we deliver the runtime and optimized kernels but they run inside your network. Kernel-level perf depends on GPU drivers and CUDA versions; we recommend validated driver stacks (we'll provide exact versions). For air-gapped, we have an installation bundle.

[09:10] Markus: Any blockers for our compliance needs? SOC/ISO, audit logs, SAML?

[09:16] Sofia: Redwood Private + Dedicated supports SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs and can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key management. We'll share the security pack.

[09:26] Alex: On model quantization — do you support QAT (quantization-aware training) pipelines or just post-training quantization?

[09:34] Daniel: We support both patterns. Post-training quantization is faster to deploy; QAT gives better accuracy but requires model retraining. We'll help with recommendations — many customers start with PTQ (post-training) for index building then evaluate QAT if recall gap too large.

[09:50] Priya: For the reranker itself — are you recommending a small cross-encoder or a dot-product MLP?

[09:56] Daniel: If latency is tight, dot-product re-ranker (dense-sim) is fastest. Small cross-encoders improve re-rank quality but add cost/latency. We often suggest trying dense-sim first (embedding similarity on full-dim) then evaluate a tuned cross-encoder for a subset of queries or for offline recalibration.

[10:18] Alex: Any empirical numbers comparing dense-sim (full-dim re-rank) vs small cross-encoder on ecomm product relevance?

[10:26] Daniel: On customer benchmarks, small cross-encoders can add 5-12% NDCG lift but at cost of 2-4x compute compared to dense-sim. If you need headroom for 100ms P95, dense-sim often wins unless you can batch heavily or run cross-encoder only on ambiguous queries.

[10:47] Priya: Ambiguous-traffic routing sounds attractive — run cross-encoder only if dense-sim score is close to threshold.

[10:55] Daniel: Exactly — a cascade approach. Also add quality monitoring; Redwood Optimize can alert on regressions tied to prompt sets and evals.

[11:05] Sofia: Let's sketch the pilot plan — Daniel?

[11:10] Daniel: Pilot steps: 1) baseline capture (current P95/throughput + dataset samples); 2) offline index builds: int8 PQ index + 768-projection index; 3) live A/B: two-stage ANN (quantized) + dense-sim re-rank on GPU; collect P95 and recall metrics; 4) iterate on batch sizes and cache TTLs; 5) security validation for VPC/KMS.

[11:34] Alex: Timeline? We want a pilot in 4-6 weeks.

[11:38] Sofia: That seems doable. Daniel, can your team run initial cluster-level benchmarks in 10 working days once we share dataset samples?

[11:46] Daniel: Yes — if you provide a 50k representative sample and traffic trace for replay. We'll run on both quantized and non-quantized configs and produce a dashboard.

[11:56] Priya: We'll provide the sample and a tiny orchestration script to replay traffic shape.

[12:02] Markus: Network constraints: everything must be inside our VPC; can you support private peering or direct connect?

[12:10] Sofia: Redwood Private supports VPC peering and private link options; we'll include network setup guides. For Dedicated hosted we can also use VPC endpoints.

[12:20] Alex: Any gotchas with cold-starts and key caching for embeddings? If we use dynamic user personalization and new vectors, index rebuilds or shaker strategies?

[12:32] Daniel: For high churn vectors you want hybrid strategies: keep a dynamic in-memory shard for recent vectors and periodically merge into main index. Our runtime supports online adds to vector indexes with background compaction. Cold-start for a newly added vector is usually small if you keep a warmed-up ANN shard.

[12:52] Priya: OK. Last technical ask: can we get a perf matrix that shows P95 latency vs batch size for both ANN and re-rank on RTX A5000 and a 48-core CPU baseline?

[13:06] Daniel: Yes — that'll be in the benchmark sheet. We'll include P50/P95 curves and memory footprints (float32 vs int8).

[13:18] Alex: Anything else on compliance or legal? I'll coordinate with Markus.

[13:22] Sofia: We'll send security docs and the SOC/ISO statements.

[13:28] Daniel: Quick note on monitoring: Redwood Console gives per-route token and vector cost breakdown; you can set alerts on P95 and per-request cost. Useful for pilot observability.

[13:40] Alex: Perfect.

[13:44] Sofia: Let's recap action items and owners.

[13:50] Alex (BlueRiver): I'll share the 50k sample, traffic trace, and security contact.

[13:56] Priya: I'll run a small local test converting 1536->768 and share a couple example deltas to show recall impact.

[14:04] Markus: I'll collect network constraints and KMS details and loop in infra.

[14:10] Daniel: We'll run the cluster benchmark and post results to the sheet within 10 business days of sample receipt.

[14:18] Sofia: We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and attach the benchmarks and security pack.

[14:26] Alex: Thanks everyone — good session.

[14:30] (meeting ends, informal chatter)
